title: Valley of Flowers National Park
selection: Valley of Flowers was published with no sections at all (a broken public page). This file fills it from the Uttarakhand Tourism destination page and Outlook Traveller's 2026 season report. Conflicts for the editor: entry fees (Outlook Traveller, 5 Jun 2026: INR 150 Indian / INR 600 foreign; several trek operators quote INR 200 / 800) and the closing date (Outlook Traveller: 31 October; PTI on 1 Jun 2026 said 'until the first fortnight of October'). Both are marked unconfirmed and block approval of the fee fact until an editor decides.

places.name: Valley of Flowers
places.summary: A UNESCO-listed alpine valley in Chamoli with over 600 flower species, reached on foot from Govindghat via Ghangaria; open June to October.
places.seoTitle: Valley of Flowers Trek Guide: Season, Permits & Route
places.seoDescription: Plan the Valley of Flowers trek: best months for blooms, 2026 season dates and entry hours, permits at Ghangaria, the Govindghat route and Hemkund Sahib.

images.alt: Green alpine meadows and river in the Valley of Flowers National Park

overview.text:
The Valley of Flowers is a high Himalayan valley in Chamoli district, protected as an 87 sq km national park. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the two core zones of the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve, alongside Nanda Devi National Park.

The valley lies at around 3,600 m. More than 600 species of flowers grow here, including orchids, poppies, primulas and anemones, among birch and rhododendron forest. Rare wildlife includes the snow leopard, black bear, red fox and Himalayan weasel. Its modern fame dates to 1931, when the British mountaineer Frank Smythe and two companions lost their way and came across it.

There are no roads into the valley. Everyone walks in from Govindghat, stays at Ghangaria and visits the valley as a day trek, because overnight stays inside the park are not allowed. It suits fit walkers, photographers and nature lovers. Many visitors combine it with the Sikh pilgrimage to Hemkund Sahib above Ghangaria.

items.title: Altitude
items.body: About 3,600 m

items.title: Area
items.body: 87 sq km national park, UNESCO World Heritage Site

items.title: Open
items.body: From 1 June to about October (2026 season)

items.title: Access
items.body: 16 km on foot from Govindghat, via Ghangaria

best_time.text:
The park opens in June, and Uttarakhand Tourism says flowers can be seen through to October, with the most blooms from July to September. Mid-July to mid-August is widely regarded as the best time. This is the height of the monsoon flowering, when the Brahma Kamal and the Himalayan blue poppy are out.

June has fewer visitors and snow lingering in parts of the valley, but the main bloom is still weeks away. In September the rain eases, the mountains are clearer and the flowers start to fade.

The flowering season is also the monsoon. Expect rain and slippery trails, and allow spare days for road closures on the way to Govindghat. For 2026 the park reopened on 1 June. Reports of the closing date differ (31 October, or the first half of October), so confirm locally.

how_to_reach.text:
Roads end at Govindghat, on the Badrinath road. The walk in is 16 km in total: about 13 km up to Ghangaria, the base village, then on into the valley the next day.

By air: Jolly Grant Airport (Dehradun) is the nearest airport. Continue by road to Govindghat.

By train: Rishikesh is the nearest railway station, 273 km from Govindghat on NH58. Take a bus or taxi from there.

By road: drive or take a bus up the Badrinath highway via Joshimath to Govindghat. Ponies and porters are available for the climb to Ghangaria.

items.title: Season
items.body: 1 June to 31 October in 2026 (one report said the first half of October). Confirm the closing date locally.

items.title: Entry hours
items.body: Entry from 7 am to 2 pm. Everyone must leave by 5 pm and be back in Ghangaria.

items.title: Entry fee
items.body: Reported for 2026 as INR 150 (Indian) and INR 600 (foreign nationals), with a permit covering up to three days. Other sources quote INR 200 and INR 800. Check at the counter.

items.title: Permit
items.body: Arrange online before arrival or buy at the Forest Department counter in Ghangaria. Carry photo ID.

items.title: Rules
items.body: No camping or overnight stays in the valley. No drones or single-use plastics.
Walk the day trek from Ghangaria into the valley meadows. Start early to make the most of the 7 am–2 pm entry window.
Photograph the July–August bloom, including the Brahma Kamal and Himalayan blue poppy.
Climb from Ghangaria to Hemkund Sahib, the Sikh shrine and lake below the Hemkund peaks.
Stop at Govindghat, where the Alaknanda and Lakshman Ganga meet, at the start of the trek.
Combine with Badrinath and Mana village, about 2 hours by taxi from Govindghat.
Join a GMVN organised trek if you prefer a guided group.

where_to_stay.text:
Ghangaria (3,050 m) is the only base for the valley, because camping and overnight stays inside the park are not allowed. It is the last village on the route with food and water, and its lodges fill up in the peak July–August season.

Govindghat and Joshimath, further down the valley, are the usual night stops before and after the trek. Joshimath is also the base for Auli.

items.body: Plan at least three nights between Govindghat and Ghangaria: walk up, valley day, then Hemkund Sahib or a spare day.
Pack rain gear and waterproof shoes: the best flowers coincide with the monsoon.
Leave Ghangaria early: entry closes at 2 pm and you must be out by 5 pm.
Carry snacks and water from Ghangaria; there are no shops inside the park.
Carry out all rubbish: single-use plastics and drones are not allowed.

items.title: Can I stay overnight in the Valley of Flowers?
items.body: No. Camping and overnight stays inside the park are not permitted, so visitors stay at Ghangaria and walk in for the day.

items.title: How long is the trek?
items.body: About 16 km from Govindghat, where the road ends. That is 13 km to Ghangaria, then on into the valley, which is visited as a day walk.

items.title: When is the best time to see the flowers?
items.body: Mid-July to mid-August is the peak bloom. The park opens in June and flowers are seen until about September–October.

items.title: Do I need a permit?
items.body: Yes. Get it online before arrival or at the Forest Department counter in Ghangaria. It is reported to cover up to three days.

items.title: Is the trek difficult?
items.body: Uttarakhand Tourism rates it moderate to challenging. Ponies and porters are available as far as Ghangaria.
